en: *Commentary on the Meaning of the Amitābha Sūtra*, composed by Huìjìng.

This *Amitābha Sūtra* is here called *Wúliàngshòu* (Immeasurable Life). It was first translated by Master Kumārajīva of the Later Qin as the *Xiǎowúliàngshòu* (Shorter Immeasurable Life); it was later retranslated by Dharma Master Guṇabhadra.

I humbly submit that the Dharma-body is formless, yet forms appear in response to the capacity for form; the Pure Land is directionless, yet directions arise through the resonance of those seeking direction.

Although the ultimate principle is profound and still, and the Way transcends names and words, through the skillful means of great compassion, [the Buddha] follows [sentient beings]—[filling in the ellipsis as appropriate]—turning the wheel of the nectar of the Dharma three times, manifesting in countless worldly realms. Those who accord with it necessarily share its source; those who are transformed may differ in their streams. Thus, Amitābha, the Awakened One, dwells in the wondrous land to propagate the Way, while Śākyamuni, the Benevolent One, abides in the Sahā world to reach out to beings. Within the Pure Land, faculties are matured and easily harmonized; within the defiled realm, the stubborn and fierce are difficult to transform. He opens the three causes to ferry the four types of birth, and spreads the nine grades to subdue the five pains.

The Buddhas of the six directions manifest throughout the trichiliocosm, attesting that rebirth there is attained; their words are not false. Because sentient beings are empty, they do not abandon great compassion; because they contemplate the Tathāgata’s quiescence, they do not lose their reverence and offerings.

Although one knows that the Buddha is quiescent and like space, yet manifests various kinds of pure buddha-fields; this may be called explaining the true reality of all phenomena without destroying conventional designations, and establishing all phenomena without moving from [the ultimate].
The *Sukhāvatīvyūha Sūtra* (The Buddha-spoken Amitābha Sūtra) is that which exhorts one to be born in the Pure Land so as not to regress from Bodhi.

Its three clarities shine like the autumn moon; its fourfold eloquence resounds like spring thunder. It praises the pure realm to demonstrate the Western Quarter and extols the supreme causes to point toward this Eastern Land. These words issue from my mouth and flow into their hearts; as awakening accords with their capacities, it is called "spoken by the Buddha."

Amitābha is translated here as "Immeasurable Life" (Wuliangshou). His radiance, his preaching of the Dharma, and his retinue are all entirely immeasurable; however, in order to attract the hearts of sentient beings, he is specifically designated by the name of his lifespan, and is thus called "Immeasurable."

The term *jing* (sūtra) has two meanings: it is glossed as "scripture" and glossed as "constant. That which is traversed by the multitude of sages is called a *jing*; that which has been constant from antiquity to the present is called "constant. Therefore, it is named the *Buddhabhāṣita Amitābha Sūtra*.
Regarding the phrase, "In this manner, he arrived at the Anāthapiṇḍada Garden," the commentary states:
The sūtra is divided into three parts:
First, the introduction; second, the main body; third, the dissemination.
Each of these three parts has two sub-divisions. Regarding the two types of introduction:
first, the general introduction for attesting to faith; second, the specific introduction for initiating the discourse.
The two aspects of the main body [of the teaching] are:
first, the causes and effects of the Land of Peace and Bliss; second, the causes and effects of Amitābha’s Dharmakāya.
The two aspects of its dissemination are:
First, when the Tathāgata had finished preaching this sutra, second, the two great assemblies rejoiced and accepted it with faith.
Regarding the general and specific introductions, each has six elements by way of analogy.
As for the six elements of the general introduction:

First, accomplishment through faith; second, accomplishment through hearing; third, accomplishment through time; fourth, accomplishment through the principal figure; fifth, accomplishment through the location; sixth, accomplishment through the assembly.
These six elements of the separate introduction shall be explained in the relevant section below.
Now, among the six components of the general introduction (*pūrvayoga*), five constitute the "accomplishment" (*siddhi*).
Such being the case, faith is established.

The term "thus" (*evam*) is an expression of faithful compliance; when there is faith, the principle of what is spoken is compliant, and when there is compliance, the way of teacher and disciple is accomplished. Whether a scripture is extensive or concise, it cannot be transmitted without faith; therefore, it is called "thus."
Furthermore, "thus" (evam) refers to the teaching; it is a definitive term. Since everything spoken by the Buddha is true, it is called "thus," and therefore it is "thus.

Moreover, one must have faith in this sutra; as the subsequent text states, the Buddhas of the six directions—like the sands of the Ganges in number—manifest signs to certify that those who practice mindfulness of Amitābha Buddha will certainly be born in the Pure Land.

At the beginning of the sutra, "Thus" indicates faith; at the end of the sutra, "joy" indicates wisdom. Faith is that which enables entry, and wisdom is that which enables transcendence. The three factors of diligence, mindfulness, and concentration form a net encompassing the beginning and the end. When the five faculties are fully perfected, one is capable of receiving and capable of transmitting [the teaching]; therefore, it says, "Thus."
Regarding "I have heard" (*evaṃ mayā śrutam*): it signifies that the hearing was accomplished.

To receive directly is called "I have heard," whereas to transmit what has been received is called "that which was heard. This indicates that one has personally received the words and meaning; specifically, it means that Ānanda personally heard from the Buddha's presence the teaching on Amitābha Buddha’s Land of Ultimate Bliss, and that those who single-mindedly recite [the name] will certainly attain rebirth there—thus ensuring there is no error of hearsay.

Before Ānanda became the attendant, he had not personally received [the teachings]; yet he says "I have heard" because the Buddha, at the time of his parinirvāṇa, gave a further brief exposition, whereby he was able to say "I have heard."
"Once upon a time" (*ekasmin samaye*) means that the time was fulfilled.

When the Buddha spoke this *Sukhāvatīvyūha Sūtra*, when Śāriputra, Ānanda, and others heard and received it, and furthermore, at the auspicious moment when the Dharma King inaugurated his mission and gathered [the assembly], it is therefore called "once upon a time."
"Buddha" means "Awakened," which signifies the primary accomplishment.
There are five types of speakers of the Dharma:
first, the Buddha; second, disciples; third, devas; fourth, immortals (ṛṣis); and fifth, emanations. Since this is spoken by the Buddha, it is called the primary accomplishment.
"Buddha" is the name for the Great Teacher, with "awakening" as its primary meaning.
There are two aspects of awakening:
first, discernment; second, enlightenment. Through enlightenment, the obstacles to knowledge are exhausted; through discernment, the obstacles of affliction are eliminated.

Regarding these two types of awakening, there are three distinctions: awakening for oneself distinguishes [the Buddha] from ordinary people; awakening others distinguishes him from those of the Two Vehicles; and the perfection of awakening distinguishes him from Bodhisattvas. When these three are complete, he is thus named "Buddha."
"Abiding" (*sthiti*) means being established in a location.
"Abiding" is also called "dwelling" (*vāsa*); there are eight types of dwelling, but here they are briefly summarized as two:
first, dwelling in the objective sphere (*viṣaya-vāsa*); second, dwelling in the basis (*āśraya-vāsa*).

Regarding "at Śrāvastī, in the Jeta Grove, Anāthapiṇḍada’s Park": this indicates the sphere of activity for the two types of practitioners; the grove serves as a place of reliance for those who remain in the secular world, while it is intended to welcome the community of renunciants.
Prince Jeta was named "Victorious in Battle" because at the time of his birth, the King defeated an enemy army; when the palace attendants reported this news, he was given this name accordingly.

Anāthapiṇḍada was originally named Sudatta; here [in China] he is called "Good Benevolence" (Shanci). He was compassionate both inwardly and outwardly and possessed great wealth; he relieved the poor and took pity on the widowed, and because the people of his village praised him for this, they gave him this name.

Among people there are distinctions of superior and inferior; one cannot first refer to it as "Jeta’s Grove" alone, for while the grove is the general term, the trees are the specific details. Nor can one speak of it collectively as "Jetavana," for two individuals joined their hearts to build this vihāra together. Because it contains both names, it is called "Jetavana Anāthapiṇḍika-ārāma."

The Dharma-body truly has no dwelling place, yet its manifestations have their methods; it provisionally resides here to teach that through the five-gate practice, one will certainly attain rebirth in the Land of Amitābha.
Regarding the five gates, the *Wangsheng lun* (Treatise on Rebirth) states:
first, the gate of prostration; second, the gate of praise; third, the gate of making vows; fourth, the gate of contemplation; and fifth, the gate of dedication.
"Accompanied by a great assembly of bhikṣus, [he went] to the various great disciples.
The commentary states:
"This refers to the formation of the assembly."
There are three assemblies:
first, the assembly of śrāvakas; second, the assembly of bodhisattvas; and third, the assembly of devas.
This assembly of śrāvakas consists of five [categories]:
First, the indication of the category; second, the proclamation of the number; third, the praise of virtues; fourth, the listing of names; fifth, the conclusion and determination.
"Together with the great bhikṣus" is the indication of the category.
"To share" (*sādhāraṇa*) is also called "common" (*sādhāraṇa*). When one’s own body and milk are simultaneously shared with another, it is termed "common.
The *Mahāprajñāpāramitā-śāstra* states:
"Sharing a single precept, a single view, a single place, and so forth, is what is called 'common'."
"Great" (Mahā) is called *mahā* in Sanskrit; it has three meanings:
first, greatness; second, abundance; and third, severance. Thus, it refers to one who is revered by humans, devas, and kings alike.
What is meant by "many"?
It refers to the number reaching one thousand two hundred and fifty, because they were able to defeat the sixteen heterodox teachers and their disputations.
There are, briefly, three meanings of the term "bhikṣu":
First, the Tamer of Māras; second, the Mendicant; third, the Destroyer of Evil—these three correspond respectively to the beginning, middle, and end.

Regarding the Tamer of Māras: when one first establishes the path of the profound gate, one immediately forms the resolve to subdue Māra; thus, at the time of first shaving the hair and donning the dyed robes, the palace of the celestial Māra trembles and Māra is struck with fear.
The "Beggar" (bhikṣu) takes his body as a vessel for the Way; since the Way flourishes when the body is at ease, he has already purchased the Dharma-robe and begs for food to sustain his body.
The "Destroyer of Evil" (prahāṇaka) means that while the Way of the sages grows and the Way of ordinary beings wanes, once what is cultivated is complete, one destroys evil to realize the fruit.

The three names of the stage of original enlightenment—namely, "Turning Fear of Māras into Slaying Thieves," "Changing the Beggar into the Worthy of Offerings," and "Explaining the Destruction of Evil as Non-arising"—constitute the attainment of the stage of fruition.
"Saṃgha" is translated here as "assembly" (zhòng); because many bhikṣus are harmoniously united in one place, it is called an assembly.
"Together with twelve hundred and fifty people" indicates the number.
The phrase "all are great arhats" is a praise of their virtue.
Regarding the three meanings of "arhat," one should understand them as being identical to the three names for the stage of fruition (phala-bhūmi) mentioned above for the bhikṣus.
"Known by all" means that the great assembly of humans and devas collectively knows their inner virtues and recognizes their outward forms.
"From the Elder Śāriputra to Aniruddha" refers to the enumeration of names, clearly listing seventeen individuals among the śrāvaka assembly.
"Elder," "Life of Wisdom" (Āyuṣmat), and "Pure Life" (Śuddhājīva) are titles by which he is praised.

Śāriputra—here translated as "Son of the Body" (Shenzi)—if his dullness had a limit, it would be a mere fragment; if his sharpness had a limit, it would be the Son of the Body. He could tell the past and know the future; his heroic talent was like a pair of hawks, and his divine wisdom was awakened through profound realization.

Maudgalyāyana is translated here as "Praise and Recitation"; Kāśyapa as "Drinker of Light"; Kauṣṭhila as "Great Knee"; Cūḍapanthaka as "Snake-Slave"; Nanda as "Joy"; Ānanda as "Delight"; Rāhula as "Obscuration"; Gavāmpati as "Bull King"; Piṇḍola as "Elder"; Phalguna as "Sharp Faculties"; Kālodayin as "Black One"; Kapphiṇa as "Lunar Mansion"; Bakula as "Good Appearance"; Aniruddha as "As One Wishes. These and others are the great disciples; this concludes the section on their fixed names.
Regarding the phrase "together with all the bodhisattvas, up to such great bodhisattvas as these," the commentary states:
This refers to the assembly of bodhisattvas, which is threefold.
First, the category is indicated; next, the names are listed; finally, the definition is concluded. A Bodhisattva is called an "Awakened Being" (*bodhisattva*);
there are four meanings of "awakening": first, that which is to be awakened to (*abhisambodhya*);
second, perfect awakening (*samyak-saṃbodhi*); third, the factors of awakening (*bodhipākṣika-dharma*); and fourth, complete awakening (*sarvabodhi*).
The term *buddha* has two meanings:
first, "to awaken" (*bodhana*), and second, "to cultivate" (*bhūṣaṇa*).
Because he awakens to phenomena and transforms sentient beings through cultivation, he is called a *buddha*, a "Great Awakened One" (*mahā-buddha*).
Paramārtha says:

Speaking in terms of stages, the ten faiths, ten understandings, and ten practices prior to the [first] ground are called the bodhisattva’s self-benefit; the stage of dedication (*pariṇāmanā*) is called the mahāsattva’s benefit for others; from the attainment of the grounds up to the seventh ground is called the bodhisattva; and from the eighth ground upward is called the mahāsattva.
The *Daśabhūmika-vibhāṣā-śāstra* states:
"There are three aspects of greatness:
first, the greatness of the vow;"
2. Greatness of Practice;
3. Greatness of Benefit.
From "Mañjuśrī" onwards, the names are listed.
Mañjuśrī, here translated as "Wondrous Virtue," is a Dharma Prince who shall succeed to the position of the Honored One.

Ajita, here translated as "Invincible," and Gandhahasti, here translated as "Red Elephant," are those of Constant Diligence, whose cultivation of the Way through body and mind is like saving one's head from fire.
“Together with such bodhisattvas as these” concludes the formal determination.
“And including Śakra Devānām Indra, up to the great assembly of devas all together”:
the commentary states:
Regarding the various classes of devas mentioned below, their full name should be Śakra Devānām Indra.
*Indra* here means "Lord" (*pati*); *devānām* here means "gods" (*deva*); and *śakra* here means "capable" (*śakya*). Thus, the collective name is "The Capable Lord of Gods."
The term "etc. includes the remainder.
Following the general introduction, the "Initiation" (nidāna) is explained; the specific introduction consists of six parts:
first, striking the responsive capacity (*tatkṣaṇa*).
2. The location; 3. The quantity; 4. The environmental retribution;
Five, the direct fruition;
six, the propagation of the teaching.
"Striking the mechanism" refers to the Buddha’s address to Śāriputra.
As for the location, it is shown to be in the western direction.
As for its magnitude, it exceeds ten million billion buddha-fields.
As for the environmental retribution, it is the Land of Ultimate Bliss.
As for the ultimate fruition, there is a Buddha there named Amitābha;
as for his propagation of the teaching, he is currently preaching the Dharma. "Śāriputra!..."
Regarding the question, "Why is that land named 'Ultimate Bliss' (*Sukhāvatī*)?",
the commentary states: Below,
the main body of the teaching is explained, briefly in two parts, in medium detail in five, and extensively in ten.
The two aspects summarized are:
first, the causes and effects of the Pure Land;
second, the causes and effects of the Dharma-body.
The five points within the middle section are:
first, clarifying the fruit of non-retrogression in Sukhāvatī through Amitābha;
second, clarifying the aspiration and practice that encourage the cultivation of its causes.
First, the Buddhas of the three times and six directions manifest signs to certify and establish [the teaching];
second, the Buddhas, having certified it, cause [beings] to practice and encourage them toward joy;
third, the World-Honored Ones of the two lands manifest signs to praise its virtues.
The ten aspects of "extensiveness" are:
first, the supportive environment of peace and happiness;
second, the primary fruition of Amitābha.
Third, the vow to be born there;
fourth, the practice for birth there;
fifth, the manifestation of signs by the Buddhas.
Sixth, the explanation of the reasons for the characteristics;
seventh, the causes of the vows throughout the three periods;
eighth, the fruits of the practices throughout the three lifetimes.
9. This Buddha praises that Buddha;
10. That Buddha praises this Buddha.
Following the latter classification, these constitute ten chapters.
First, the explanation of the environmental rewards (*pratyaya-sampad*) of Sukhāvatī has two parts:
first, the question;
second, the answer. This is the question.
Regarding the passage, "The sentient beings of that land have no manifold sufferings... therefore it is named 'Ultimate Bliss,'" this is the response, which has two parts:
first, a brief answer that establishes the thesis; second, an extensive explanation that unfolds the thesis.
This is the brief response that establishes the fundamental tenet.

In that Land of Amitābha, there are no manifold sufferings, but only matters of joy; once born in that land, one transversely cuts off the five paths of rebirth, transcends the triple world, and reaches the stage of non-retrogression, having fulfilled the cultivation of ten thousand kalpas during the first asaṃkhyeya-aeon.
The *Daśabhūmika-vibhāṣā-śāstra* states:
"There are two types of cultivation of the path:
first, that which is difficult to practice;"
2. Easy Practice.

Cultivating the Path in this land is called "difficult practice," whereas cultivating the Path in the Western Land is called "easy practice. It is like a person with a lameness who suffers when walking on land, yet finds joy when traveling by boat on water.
"Furthermore, Śāriputra, as for the statement that 'the Land of Ultimate Bliss has sevenfold railings extending to what is called Ultimate Bliss,' the commentary states:"
The following clarifies the opening of the school, which consists of five broad expositions:

first, the adornment of the jeweled railings and groves; second, the adornment of the jeweled ponds and the radiance of flowers; third, the adornment of the jewels of bliss and supernormal powers; fourth, the adornment of the Dharma-sounds of the jeweled birds; and fifth, the adornment of the jeweled trees swaying in the wind.
This is the first Array of the Jewel Balustrade Forest, which has six features:
first, the jewel balustrades; second, the jewel railings; third, the jewel lattice forest; and sixth, the array of jewel trees.

The inner virtues are maintained by the balustrades, while the outer world is protected by the railings; the net of vows is bound with cords of pearls—the dharmas free from outflows—and the grove of *zhi* herbs represents the adornment of the realm through the meritorious dharmas of the Western [Pure Land].
Regarding the passage, "Furthermore, Śāriputra, from the Land of Ultimate Bliss to the Adornment of Meritorious Virtues," the commentary states:
Second, the Adornment of the Radiant Flowers of the Jewel Ponds has eight aspects:

First, jeweled ponds; second, jeweled waters; third, jeweled steps; fourth, jeweled paths; fifth, jeweled towers; sixth, jeweled pavilions; seventh, jeweled flowers; eighth, the adornment of jeweled light, and so forth.

The pond is the bathing pool of the eight liberations; the water is the fragrant water of the eight virtues; the pavilions are the lofty towers of the eight concentrations; the galleries are the multi-storied halls of the three emptinesses; the flowers are the awakening blossoms of the seven purities; and the light is the radiance of wisdom, capable of destroying the darkness of ignorance born from doubt.
"Furthermore, Śāriputra,
'constantly performing celestial music until reaching the Adornment of Merit'.
Commentary states:
The third is the adornment of the joy of the jewels and supernormal powers, which has three parts:
first, manifesting the creation of joy and the raining of flowers; second, manifesting the making of offerings to all Buddhas; and third, manifesting the accomplishment of the array of ornaments.

The heavens rained down the four kinds of flowers throughout the six periods of the day, while humans from the ten directions made offerings to the myriad Buddhas; at dawn, they would perform those acts of worship, and at mealtime, they would come from there to this place to practice walking meditation.
"Furthermore, Śāriputra, as for the statement that 'in that land there are always various kinds of birds produced by transformation,'" the commentary states:
The fourth section, "The Multitude of Precious Birds Adorned with the Sound of the Dharma," has six parts:

first, a general indication of the auspicious birds; second, the specific enumeration of their names; third, the chanting of the sound of the Dharma; fourth, hearing and recollecting the Three Jewels; fifth, the dispelling of doubts and attachments; and sixth, the manifestation of the inconceivable.
"Various wonderful birds of mixed colors" is a general designation for auspicious birds of extraordinary hues.
"White cranes, peacocks, and *saṃjīva* birds" specifically names them, briefly enumerating the names of these seven types of birds.

Regarding the phrase "expounding throughout the six periods the dharmas of the faculties, powers, factors of awakening, and so forth": the Dharma-Buddha constantly contemplates the sentient beings of the six realms during the six periods, and the birds likewise sing praises of the factors of the path (mārga-aṅga) during those same six periods.
Regarding the passage, “When the sentient beings of that land hear this sound, they all bring to mind the Buddha, the Dharma, and the Sangha,” this clarifies the benefit for those who hear it.

As for the passage, “Śāriputra, do not say that these birds are actually born as a result of karmic retribution, let alone [that they have] actual [existence],” this serves to dispel emotional doubts; first, it restates the nature of the doubt.
The section beginning with "Therefore" provides the explanation: in that land, even the names of the three evil realms do not exist, let alone the actual conditions of the three evil realms.
The phrase "all these... produced by transformations" reveals its inconceivability.
"These birds, Śāriputra, are actually emanated by Amitābha to proclaim the sound of the Dharma, to adorn the realm, and to benefit sentient beings."
Regarding the phrase, "In that Buddha-land, a subtle breeze blows and moves [the trees], resulting in such adornments," the commentary states:
Fifth, the solemnity of the jewel-trees swaying in the wind has four aspects:
First, the sound of trees shaken by the wind; second, like the music of celestial deities; third, hearing and reciting the Three Refuges; fourth, the accomplishment of adornment.
Regarding "a gentle breeze blowing upon the rows of various precious trees": when the wind shakes the precious trees, it is the Dharma preaching wondrous sounds.
For example, the hundred thousand kinds of music, with sounds like those of celestial music, serve as a metaphor for wondrous sound.
That "hearers simultaneously recollect the Buddha, Dharma, and Sangha" clarifies that hearing and recollecting the Three Refuges constitutes the benefit for the hearers.
"One who accomplishes such merit" refers to the accomplishment of the Adornment-Union (vyūha-siddhi).
"Śāriputra, as for your thought regarding Amitābha... [and so forth].
The commentary states:
The following clarifies the second section, the primary retribution of Amitābha, which has four parts:
first, the question; second, the answer; third, the conclusion; and fourth, the determination of the stages.
Regarding this question, why is he named Amitābha?
"Śāriputra, as for that Buddha’s radiance... [it is said].
The commentary states: This is the answer.
There are three parts to the answer:
"First, his radiance; second, his lifespan; third, his assembly—this radiance is immeasurable.
Furthermore, Śāriputra, 'his lifespan extends to ten kalpas from now.'"
The commentary states:
This clarifies that his lifespan is immeasurable, first in a general sense and then in a specific sense.

Generally, the lifespans of his assembly are immeasurable; specifically, it refers only to Amitābha’s own lifespan. Although his life spans ten kalpas, because these cannot be calculated or known by the world, it is called "Immeasurable Life."
"Furthermore, Śāriputra!
That Buddha has immeasurable and boundless [qualities], and it is the same for all the bodhisattvas.
The commentary states:
Explaining the assembly of followers.
There are two types of followers:
first, the assembly of śrāvakas, which consists of those on the four stages of approach and the four fruits of realization; [the second is the assembly of bodhisattvas].

As for the two assemblies of bodhisattvas, namely the fifty-two worthies, they together rain down the majesty of the provisional and the real, and uniformly grasp the principles of the vehicles. "Śāriputra!
Up to the accomplishment of such adornments of merit" means:
The commentary states:
This is a brief conclusion.
Although the radiance, lifespan, bodhisattvas, śrāvakas, persons, and dharmas differ from one another, they all transcend the reach of calculation; therefore, they are called "immeasurable."
It is named according to its origin; therefore, it is called "Immeasurable Life.
Furthermore, Śāriputra, regarding those born in the land of Sukhāvatī, even if one were to speak for incalculable eons (*asaṃkhyeya-kalpa*), [the number would not be exhausted].
The commentary states:
Next, the determination of stages is explained with three points:
first, that in that land one is already an *avaivartika* (non-retrogressive), which clarifies the strength of the cause;...
Second, there are many Bodhisattvas who are in their final birth before Buddhahood; this clarifies the excellence of the conditions.
Third, it is spoken over incalculable eons (*asaṃkhyeya-kalpa*); this clarifies the greatness of the assembly. "Śāriputra!..."
Regarding the phrase, "Sentient beings who hear this should make a vow to go together to one place," the commentary states:
The following clarifies the third [stage], the making of the vow for rebirth; first is the heading, followed by the explanation.
Sentient beings have no fixed expectation; they may attain realization midway, set their minds upon the ultimate fruit, or not be drawn back into rebirth midway.
"Śāriputra, one cannot be born in that land by means of small roots of goodness or merit" means:
The commentary states:
The following clarifies the fourth practice, that of rebirth; it consists first of a heading, second of an explanation, and finally of a conclusion.
This is the heading for the practice.
It is because they have long cultivated roots of goodness that they are born there; therefore, it is said that they are not few. "Śāriputra!
If good men and good women hear the name of Amitābha Buddha and are born in the Land of Ultimate Bliss..."
The commentary states:
"Shi" (釋) refers to practice, which has five aspects:
first, the single principle; second, the fundamental name; third, the temporal division; fourth, that Buddha coming here to welcome; and fifth, being born there from this life.
The mechanism refers to men and women;
the fundamental name refers to Amitābha Buddha;
the period of time refers to seven days of single-minded devotion.
If that Buddha comes here to welcome one, it means the holy assembly of Amitābha descends to receive one at the end of life;
if one is born there from this life, it means that because the mind is not inverted, one attains rebirth there immediately.
"Śāriputra! I see this benefit as leading to the arousal of inconceivable merit.
The commentary states:
Regarding the "binding": first, one binds the preceding vow; second, one binds the subsequent practice.

Once born in that land, one will certainly attain the stage of non-retrogression; crossing transversely across the five paths of existence, one directly transcends the triple world. Although the river of birth and death is dark, one will cross it before long; although the path to nirvana is distant, one may yet ascend it. Therefore, it is said: "Seeing these benefits."

"Śāriputra! As for my current praise of the benefits of inconceivable merit," this concludes the subsequent practice; it also serves as a sign of the harmonious connection between what precedes and what follows, thereby establishing their mutual proof.
Regarding the passage, "In the east there is also the Buddha Akṣobhya, and so on up to the Buddhas of the zenith who protect and mind this sutra," the commentary states:
The fifth [section] clarifies that the Buddhas of the six directions manifest signs to provide authentic testimony.
The six directions consist of the four cardinal directions, the zenith, and the nadir; they demonstrate the place where Buddhahood is realized.

The Buddhas refer to the myriad types of awakening throughout the three periods of time and the three bodies, as numerous as the sands of the Ganges; they clarify that one who realizes Buddhahood is a person.
The manifestation of signs is the extending of the tongue so that it pervades the three thousandfold world system;
this is the sign of clear verification. To speak words of sincerity as a means of verification is the teaching of established proof.
The text contains six directions, which constitute six layers; within each direction, there are likewise four points.

Regarding the four points of the eastern direction: first, the place of testimony, which is the east; second, the persons who testify, namely the Buddhas such as Akṣobhya, as numerous as the sands of the Ganges; third, the testimony of signs, wherein the tongue [of the Buddha] pervades the trichiliocosm; and fourth, the testimony of the teaching, which is that one should believe this sutra.

When disciples preach the sutras, they cite their own disciples as witnesses; when the Buddhas preach the sutras, they take the Buddhas themselves as witnesses. Therefore, [the text] cites the Buddhas of the six directions, as numerous as the sands of the Ganges, who extend their tongues and speak words of truth: "If one recites the name of Amitābha, one will certainly attain rebirth in that Land of Ultimate Bliss and reach the stage of non-retrogression. The remaining five directions and four gates may be understood by analogy with this.
"Śāriputra! What do you think regarding the passage 'up to the Sūtra on Protective Recollection'?
The commentary states:
The following clarifies the reason for the sixth explanation of the characteristics; first there is the question, followed by the answer.
This is the question: "Śāriputra!..."
"If a son or daughter of good family attains to *samyak-saṃbodhi*," it is said:
this is the answer.

"Whoever hears the name of this sutra, as well as the names of Amitābha and the other Buddhas, and is able to uphold them without forgetting, shall be protected by all Buddhas and shall never regress from Bodhi. Therefore, Śāriputra!"
"Ye all should believe and accept my words, as well as those spoken by all Buddhas.
The commentary states:
This clarifies the seventh cause for the vow made at the three times.
The text consists of two parts:

first, the command to listen with faith and acceptance; second, the formal elucidation of the causes for the vows of the three periods. This [section] is the command to listen with faith and acceptance.
"My words" refers to Śākyamuni’s exhortation to be born in the Pure Land.
Regarding the phrase "spoken by all Buddhas," it means that the Buddhas of the six directions, as numerous as the sands of the Ganges, exhort and certify one's rebirth there. "Śāriputra!
If there is anyone who has already made the vow to reach supreme enlightenment... [and so forth].
The commentary states:
"This precisely clarifies the vows for the three periods.
Those who have already made these vows include those such as Avalokiteśvara, Mahāsthāmaprāpta, and Nāgārjuna."
"Those who make the vow now" refers to those of the present generation who receive it with faith.
"Those who shall make the vow" refers to the classes of beings who will have faith in the future.
"Those who wish to be born in the land of Amitābha Buddha" refers to the places where they will be born according to their vows made during the three periods [of past, present, and future].

Regarding "those who attain non-retrogressive bodhi": having been born in that place once, because the land is superior and the conditions are powerful, they will certainly ascend to the stage of non-retrogressive, unsurpassed bodhi.
As for the phrase "in that land... up to being born in that land."
The commentary states:
"Below, it clarifies the fruit of the third birth of the eighth stage.
Those who have already been born refer to those such as Avalokiteśvara and Mahāsthāmaprāpta."
"Those born now" refers to those who currently believe and accept [the teaching].
"Those to be born" refers to the class of beings who will be born in the future through belief and acceptance.

Since both sages of the past and saints of the future all vow to be born there, one who observes the worthy and aspires to equal them should, if they possess faith, likewise resolve to be born in that land.
"The reason all Buddhas earnestly and repeatedly exhort [beings] to return to the Western Land is that there one will certainly attain non-retrogression. Śāriputra!
As for my own present arrival at inconceivable merit..."
The commentary states:

The following clarifies the ninth [section], wherein this Buddha praises that [other Buddha]. This refers to Śākyamuni Tathāgata praising the fruits of the pure lands of Amitābha and all other Buddhas, saying:
"Those Buddhas have attained matters that are exceedingly difficult to encounter and rare."
The commentary states:
Next, the tenth section clarifies that this Buddha praises Śākyamuni’s accomplishment of the path within this defiled land as a difficult feat.

This "difficult feat" refers to teaching and transforming sentient beings in the world of the five turbidities, leading them to have faith and take refuge in the Pure Land, and ensuring they attain the stage of non-retrogression with certainty.
The text has three layers:
first, the heading; second, the explanation; and third, the conclusion.
The heading refers to matters that are extremely difficult and rare; "extremely difficult" comprises three chapters.
The second explanation concerns the matter of awakening amidst the five turbidities;
the third conclusion returns to summarize these three meanings.
This constitutes the heading: first general, then specific.
In general, this clarifies the merits of that Buddha’s meditation and my own; specifically, it concerns matters that are extremely difficult and rare.
"Extremely difficult" refers to the five turbidities of the evil world; "rare matters" refers to the matter of unsurpassed bodhi, which he then expounded for the sake of the assembly.
"To preach for the sake of the multitude that by cultivating causes in this defiled land one attains the fruit of a pure land—this is a dharma difficult to realize.
Regarding the phrase, "one who is able [to teach] the most difficult-to-believe dharma in the Sahā world-system":
The commentary states:
The explanation of the three chapters begins with the "Five Turbidities," which explains the chapter heading on "Extreme Difficulty.
"Attaining Bodhi" explains the chapter heading on "Rarity."
"To preach for the sake of sentient beings" refers to the topical outline of the section on the Buddha’s deeds. "Śāriputra!
You should know that what I have done up to this point is extremely difficult."
The commentary states:
This concludes the three chapters.
Regarding the attainment of bodhi amidst the five turbidities, these two sections conclude the section on self-benefit.
"To speak for the sake of all the world" refers to the benefit of others (*parārtha*) summarized under one heading. Regarding the phrase,
"After the Buddha had spoken this sutra, [the assembly] attained joy and accepted it with faith," the commentary states:
The propagation [of this teaching] is clarified.
As the two sages engage in mutual exaltation, the fourfold assembly receives benefit; with deep hearts of joy, they accept it in faith and practice accordingly.
The *Commentary on the Meaning of the Amitābha Sūtra* concludes.
